lesson.title: The Repeating Geometry That Holds a Salt Together
lesson.summary: A crystal lattice is the orderly, repeating three dimensional arrangement of ions in an ionic solid, and the enormous energy released when that lattice assembles, the lattice energy, is what ultimately makes ionic compounds stable.
lesson.body:
An ionic compound is not a loose pile of cations and anions, it is an extremely orderly, repeating three dimensional pattern called a crystal lattice, in which each ion occupies a fixed position relative to its neighbors and is surrounded by a specific, predictable number of oppositely charged ions, called its coordination number. In sodium chloride, each Na+ ion is surrounded by six Cl- ions at the corners of an octahedron, and each Cl- ion is likewise surrounded by six Na+ ions, giving a coordination number of six for both. This precise, repeating geometry is not arbitrary, it is the specific arrangement that lets ions of opposite charge sit as close together as possible while keeping ions of the same charge as far apart as possible, which maximizes the attractive forces and minimizes the repulsive ones throughout the entire structure.

The energy released when a crystal lattice assembles from its separate gas phase ions is called lattice energy, defined as the energy released in the process Na+(g) plus Cl-(g) yields NaCl(s). Because it measures pure electrostatic attraction, lattice energy follows directly from Coulomb's law: the attraction between two charges is proportional to the product of their charges divided by the distance between them. This is why lattice energy depends so strongly on ionic charge and size. Sodium chloride, built from singly charged Na+ and Cl- ions, has a lattice energy of about negative 787 kilojoules per mole. Magnesium oxide, built from doubly charged Mg2+ and O2- ions that are also somewhat smaller than sodium and chloride ions, has a far larger lattice energy, roughly negative 3800 kilojoules per mole, nearly five times greater, since doubling both charges roughly quadruples the electrostatic attraction on its own, before even accounting for the shorter ion to ion distance.

Lattice energy is the missing piece that finally makes the full energy story of ionic bond formation add up. Forming gas phase Na+ and Cl- ions from neutral sodium and chlorine atoms actually costs a net 147 kilojoules per mole, since sodium's ionization energy of 496 kilojoules per mole is larger than the 349 kilojoules per mole released by chlorine's electron affinity. That deficit would make ionic compound formation look unfavorable if the story stopped there. But the ions do not remain separate gas phase particles, they immediately come together and release their full lattice energy, about 787 kilojoules per mole for sodium chloride, as they lock into the crystal lattice. That release overwhelms the earlier 147 kilojoule per mole cost many times over, which is exactly why sodium metal and chlorine gas react to form solid sodium chloride so readily and so exothermically.

This same lattice energy dependence on charge and size explains the extreme physical properties of compounds like magnesium oxide compared to sodium chloride. Because magnesium oxide's ions are held together by an attraction roughly five times stronger, its melting point climbs to about 2852 degrees Celsius, far above sodium chloride's 801 degrees Celsius, which is why magnesium oxide is used as a refractory material in furnace linings that must survive extreme heat. The crystal lattice, and the lattice energy that holds it together, is the final link connecting everything in this unit: ionization energy and electron affinity set the cost of forming ions, electronegativity predicts whether ions form at all, and lattice energy, governed by the same charge and size relationships, determines whether the resulting solid is barely stable or nearly indestructible.
